newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: FEATURE - Little England perched in Sri Lankan hil.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Little England perched in Sri Lankan hil.

text.p: At the Hill Club the ladies were not permitted in the billiard room until 1960 -- and they were still only allowed to use the side entrance.
Victoria Park gets seedlings from London's Kew Gardens and the gardener boasts: "We have been growing plants for British kings and queens for 150 years."

Sri Lanka may have won its independence from Britain in 1948 but Nuwara Eliya, a genteel hill station perched high in tea plantation country, still stands as a "Little England" monument half a century later.

Tudor-style mansions and Victorian homes are dotted around the slopes of Nuwara Eliya, perched in crisp, cool air 6,128 feet (1,884 metres) above the sweltering heat and cloying humidity of the plains. BRITISH COLONISER PUTS HILL STATION ON THE MAP
Outside the quaint pink-and-white post office stands an 1829 mail box still bearing the royal crest.
The invigorating climate prompted the British in 1825 to set up a health resort and military sanatorium in Nuwara Eliya.

But it was explorer Sir Samuel Baker, best known for discovering the source of the White Nile, who really put the place on the map. In 1846 he decided to turn Nuwara Eliya into an English village in the tropics.
Baker was typical of the indefatigable coloniser who "painted the map pink" for Britain with missionary zeal and helped build an empire of 400 million people around the world.

He used bullock wagons and elephant carts to drag an instant English village up the Ramboda Pass -- a pack of foxhounds, farmhands, a blacksmith, a bailiff, herds of Hereford and Durham cows. HILL CLUB LIKE STEPPING INTO A TIME WARP
Today the legacies of those colonisers still stand. Sri Lankans look on the past with affection. Colonial vestiges have not been swept away.
When the English tea planters found that membership had sunk to an all-time low at the Hill Club, they finally admitted Sri Lankans for the first time in 1967.
Today it is like stepping into a time warp.
A crackling log fire heats the reading room. You can sink into leather armchairs with a musty volume picked from its venerable shelves.
The walls are dotted with the heads of deer and leopard. Above the fireplace hangs a portrait of the now divorced Prince Charles and Princess Diana.
Next door stands the Men Only Bar. Ladies may sip cocktails only in the Mixed Bar. Ties and jackets are compulsory for gentlemen at the candle-lit dinner table.
The old complaints book is dotted with colonials venting their spleen.
In 1902 a Mr P.P. Blackmore complained: "Would suggest use of Bromo toilet paper in the closets in place of the present stuff, which is like cardboard."

Next door stands the Grand Hotel, an elegant Elizabethan pile that was once the summer residence of the 19th Century Governor of Ceylon, Sir Edward Barnes. It was the setting for the annual Government Ball when colonial High Society was out in force.
Twenty live brown trout survived the passage from England and prospered in Lake Gregory that fringes the hill station.
Today a tethered pony grazes by the winning post on the rundown racecourse while boys play cricket in the paddock.
But the place springs alive in the April High Season with fiercely contested pony races. PARK DOTTED WITH ELEGANT BRITISH PLANTS
Victoria Park, dotted with azaleas and forget-me-not's, offers the perfect place for an evening constitutional.
Tony Wija Sinha, heading a battalion of 45 gardeners, proudly shows off this tropical replica of an English country garden.
"It was all started for Queen Victoria 154 years ago. Look at these sweet williams, see the camellias. All our plants are English," he said of a legacy that lives on.
And a nearby cemetery concludes with an ironic twist of fate. There lies buried Major Thomas Rogers, a famed great white hunter who killed 1,500 elephants in his time.
He was never trampled under foot by his victims but died when killed by a bolt of lightning. Since then, his grave has twice been struck by lightning.
